plain: When people say a dinner "smacks" of something, they mean it strongly suggests or carries a distinct trace of that quality, usually a flavor. If a dish smacks of garlic, garlic is clearly the dominant taste. The phrase can also describe a less desirable trait, the way a menu might smack of laziness if every dish is simply reheated. Separately, in casual slang, "that dinner smacks" simply means it tasted excellent or hit the spot, with no comparison implied at all. Context decides which sense applies: older or formal usage tends to mean "smacks of X," pointing at a specific quality, while modern slang on its own usually just means the food was delicious.

plain: Grover Cleveland is the only U.S. president to serve two non-consecutive terms. He won the presidency in 1884, lost his re-election bid to Benjamin Harrison in 1888, then ran again in 1892 and won, returning to the White House after four years out of office. That's why he's counted twice in the official numbering, as both the 22nd and 24th president, even though he's really just one person. His comeback remains unique in American history; no other president has managed to leave office after an election loss and later reclaim the position in a later election. Historians often bring up his case whenever a modern politician talks about attempting something similar decades later.

plain: From a purely logical standpoint, the "nature of God" is usually approached through a short list of proposed attributes: omniscience, omnipotence, omnibenevolence, and often necessary existence, meaning God's existence wouldn't depend on anything else. Philosophers debate whether these attributes are even mutually consistent; the classic paradox asks whether an omnipotent being can create a stone too heavy for it to lift. Logic alone can't prove or disprove God's existence, but it can test whether a proposed definition holds together internally without contradiction. Different traditions define these attributes differently, so a logical analysis of "God" really depends heavily on which specific definition or theological framework you start from before evaluating consistency or implications.

plain: Late spring through early fall, roughly May through September, is generally considered the best time to visit Chicago. Summer brings warm, comfortable temperatures perfect for exploring the lakefront, Millennium Park, and outdoor festivals like Taste of Chicago and the Air and Water Show. September is a favorite for many locals because the crowds thin out while the weather stays pleasant. Spring can be unpredictable and still chilly, and winters are famously harsh and windy, with temperatures often dropping well below freezing. If you want fewer tourists and lower hotel prices while still getting decent weather, aim for early June or September rather than the peak of July and August.

plain: "It's" is always a contraction, short for "it is" or "it has" — for example, "it's raining" means "it is raining." "Its" without the apostrophe is a possessive pronoun, showing that something belongs to it, as in "the dog wagged its tail." The confusion happens because apostrophes usually signal possession elsewhere, like "Sarah's book," but pronouns break that pattern; think of "his" or "hers," which also have no apostrophe. A quick test is to mentally expand the word: if you can substitute "it is" or "it has" and the sentence still makes sense, use "it's"; otherwise, use "its" instead every time.

plain: Laika, a stray dog from Moscow, was the first animal to orbit Earth, launched aboard the Soviet spacecraft Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. She was found on the streets and selected partly because strays were assumed to be hardier and better at enduring harsh, cramped conditions than pets. Unfortunately, the spacecraft was never designed to bring her back, and she died within hours of launch due to overheating, a fact the Soviet Union didn't publicly admit until decades later. Her flight proved that a living creature could survive the launch and initial period of weightlessness, paving the way for later human spaceflight missions.

plain: Research on four-day workweek trials, including large pilots in the UK and Iceland, suggests many companies can maintain or even improve output with one fewer working day, as long as the switch comes with real changes to how time is used, not just cramming the same work into fewer hours. Reported benefits include lower stress, better focus, reduced burnout, and similar or higher productivity per hour worked. Results vary a lot by industry, though; roles requiring constant coverage, like healthcare or retail, are harder to compress than office-based knowledge work. So it can work, but success depends heavily on the type of job, how meetings and workflows are restructured, and genuine buy-in from management.

plain: A simple, low-pressure way to start a conversation with a stranger is to comment on something in your shared environment, like the weather, a long line, or an event you're both attending, since it gives an easy, natural opening. Follow up with a genuine open-ended question, such as asking what brought them there or what they think of the place, rather than something that only invites a yes-or-no answer. Keep your body language open and make brief eye contact so you come across as approachable rather than intrusive. Smiling first helps a lot too. If the person seems receptive, gradually ask more personal questions; if they seem closed off, it's fine to politely let it go.

plain: The interior angles of any triangle always add up to exactly 180 degrees, regardless of the triangle's shape or size, whether it's equilateral, isosceles, scalene, right, acute, or obtuse. You can prove it by drawing a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and using the properties of alternate angles formed by that line and the triangle's other two sides. Interestingly, this rule changes on curved surfaces: on a sphere, for example, a triangle's angles can add up to more than 180 degrees, part of what defines non-Euclidean geometry.

plain: To make a classic Long Island Iced Tea, combine half an ounce each of vodka, gin, white rum, tequila, and triple sec in a shaker or directly over ice in a tall glass. Top the glass off with a splash of cola, which gives the drink its signature tea-like color, and stir gently again. Garnish with a lemon wedge.
